vignette: Arthur Vance was fifty-two when the explosion tore through the municipal transit terminal, the blast wave throwing him against a concrete pillar while glass rained down like shrapnel. The world narrowed to burnt rubber and blood in his mouth. He remembered the exact sequence—the sudden roar, the deafening silence that followed, the way strangers’ faces contorted in the same uniform mask of shock. Over the years, Arthur found he could not piece the afternoon together into a straight line. He would try to lay out what happened, but the pieces refused to align. He could not tell a clear story of what happened even to himself, and that silence between the gaps grew heavier each day. He had come to believe that somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, that someone else would have moved sooner, that his presence there was a mistake. He also carried a quiet, unrelenting certainty that he had failed in his most important role, though he rarely named it. The years that followed did not soften the clarity of what remained. When sleep slipped away or a sudden screech of tires broke his concentration, the memories arrived fully formed and detailed, every shadow and flicker of light preserved as if etched into glass. Yet on other days, when his wife, Eleanor, asked him gently to talk about it, the recollection would drain of all feeling. He would sit across from her and describe the terminal with the flat tone of a man reading from a ledger, his voice steady while his chest went hollow, as if he could recall what happened but felt completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger. He never tried to bridge the two states; he simply moved through the room, alternately overwhelmed by what remained sharp and hollowed out by what had gone quiet. At seventy-one, Arthur kept his job as a security guard at a community recreation center, a position that demanded quiet observation and a steady presence. The post he held at the front desk became a carefully negotiated arrangement: he always sat with his back against the plaster wall, so that every person who crossed the threshold entered his sight line first. He watched the lobby with a quiet, unblinking attention, cataloging gait and posture, vigilant for dangerous people. A heavy duffel bag left unattended near the coat rack sent his pulse quickening; a man in a long coat speaking too loudly on a phone made Arthur’s shoulders tighten. He told himself he was just doing his job, but what frightened him most was the certainty that the wrong kind of person could slip past his notice, that the terminal’s silence could return without warning. When the days grew long and the center emptied, Arthur’s mind circled back to the same fixed point. He sat in his armchair after Eleanor went to bed and let his thoughts run toward the men who had done it, replaying scenarios in his head, ruminating about how to get even with the assailant. The more he turned those thoughts over, the more exhausted he felt by morning, and the smallest disruptions—a late grocery delivery, a flickering streetlight, Eleanor’s tired sigh over the bills—left him unable to deal with even the slightest upset. His hands would tremble, his breath would catch, and he would retreat to the spare room until the wave passed. For months, this had been the rhythm of his life, the quiet accumulation of habits that kept him functioning but slowly narrowed his world. What finally brought him to sit in the therapist’s office was the morning Eleanor quietly packed a weekend bag and told him she needed space, that she loved him but could not keep walking on eggshells. Arthur did not know how to fix it, only that he was tired of carrying the weight alone, and that he hoped, somehow, to find a way to sit in a room without bracing for what might come next.
